BacktestRunOut.description:
The header of one backtest run.

``id``, ``started_at`` and ``finished_at`` are null only in the worker's
``--format json --no-save`` output, where no run row exists. A stored run
always carries all three.
BacktestRunOut.title: BacktestRunOut

CalibrationBin.description:
One equal-width calibration bin of one model and outcome.

An empty bin (``n = 0``) has no mean prediction and no observed frequency;
the database stores that as two NULLs and this DTO states the same rule.
The four floats are probabilities or probability bin edges, so each one is
finite and inside ``0..1``, and the two edges are ordered.
CalibrationBin.title: CalibrationBin

CommonSubset.description:
The metrics of every model on the matches they all predicted.

Only this subset compares models fairly: the ``models`` list of the
response is computed on each model's own scored rows, which may differ.

match_count.description: The size of the shared match set.
match_count.title: Match Count

models.description: One entry per model, in the requested model order.
models.title: Models

CommonSubset.title: CommonSubset

FieldError.description:
One reason a request body or a query string was rejected.

``loc`` is the path of the offending value inside the request, ``msg`` is
the human-readable reason and ``type`` is the stable machine-readable kind.
The rejected input itself is never echoed: it is untrusted data and may be
large.
FieldError.title: FieldError

FormSummary.description:
The recent form of one team, with the matches it was read from.

``results`` holds one letter per match, newest first: ``W``, ``D`` or ``L``
from this team's point of view. ``matches`` is the same matches in the same
order, so a client can render the result next to the fixture it came from
without a second request. ``results`` and ``matches`` therefore always have
the same length.

``points``, ``goals_for`` and ``goals_against`` are the totals over exactly
these matches, not over the season: the caller decides which matches the
summary covers, so the same shape serves the last five fixtures of a season
and the fixtures before a given kickoff.
FormSummary.title: FormSummary

HeadToHead.description:
The prior meetings of the two clubs of the fixture, and their record.

``played`` counts every prior meeting of the pair, at either venue, dated
strictly before the fixture's own kickoff date. ``matches`` lists only the
ten most recent of those meetings, newest first, because a league pair meets
twice a season and a long rivalry would otherwise dominate the payload. The
two fields are therefore not the same length and ``played`` may exceed
``len(matches)``: a client that renders the record reads the counters, and a
client that renders the recent meetings reads the list.

The three counters are seen from *this fixture's* home side, not from the
venue of each earlier meeting: :attr:`home_side_wins` counts the meetings
the home team of this fixture won, :attr:`away_side_wins` the ones its
opponent won, and :attr:`draws` the ones neither won, whatever end of the
ground each club played at. A venue-based count would describe the home
teams of the earlier meetings instead, which is a different club in half of
them.
HeadToHead.title: HeadToHead

IngestionRejectionOut.description:
One source row a loader refused, with the reason it gave.

``raw`` is the stored JSON object of the refused row, so a client renders
the values the loader saw without a second request. The column holds a JSON
object, and the payload types it as one rather than as an arbitrary JSON
value, because that is what every stored row is.
IngestionRejectionOut.title: IngestionRejectionOut

IngestionRunDetail.description:
One recorded run with the rejections it kept.

``rejections_total`` is the number of rejected rows the run recorded, which
is the count of every rejection row and not necessarily the size of
``rejections``: the embedded list is capped, so a client compares the two to
tell a complete list from a truncated one.
IngestionRunDetail.title: IngestionRunDetail

IngestionRunOut.description:
One recorded loader run.

``season_code`` is the season code the loader was asked to ingest, not a
season identifier: the column is plain text with no foreign key, so a run of
a season that is no longer stored stays readable.

Every counter is the number of rows the loader read, upserted, removed,
withdrew and rejected in that run, and none of them is null: a zero means
the loader counted none, which is not the same as a count it did not record.
IngestionRunOut.title: IngestionRunOut

IngestionRunPage.description:
One page of recorded runs.

The generic envelope is specialised here so the generated client and the
OpenAPI document name a concrete schema, ``IngestionRunPage``, instead of an
anonymous generic.
IngestionRunPage.title: IngestionRunPage

LiveMetricsResponse.description:
The live metrics report: per-model scores, the common subset and counts.

The response exists so the API and the worker report share one shape. The
``models`` list is per model and may cover different match sets, ``common``
is the fair comparison and is null when no match is shared, and
``market_reference`` is null when no odds are available.

common.description: The shared-match comparison, null when no match is shared.

counts.description: The outcome counts of the evaluated rows.

evaluated_as_of.description: The Madrid date the report was evaluated at.
evaluated_as_of.title: Evaluated As Of

market_reference.description: The market benchmark, null when no odds are available.

LiveMetricsResponse.title: LiveMetricsResponse

MarketReference.description:
The market as a reference, scored on the same stored-prediction rows.

The odds are pre-kickoff information, so the market price is a legitimate
comparison. It was not stored live, though: the reference is recomputed from
the odds of a played match, which means it is a benchmark, not a prediction
the worker stored before kickoff. ``stored_before_kickoff`` is therefore
always ``False`` and never claims otherwise.

match_count.description: The number of matches the reference covers.
match_count.title: Match Count

matches_without_odds.description: The matches the reference had to skip for missing odds.
matches_without_odds.title: Matches Without Odds

stored_before_kickoff.description: Always false: the reference is recomputed, not a stored live row.
stored_before_kickoff.title: Stored Before Kickoff

MarketReference.title: MarketReference

MatchDetail.description:
One fixture with its statistics.

``stats`` is ``None`` when the match has no statistics row, which is the
normal state of a fixture that has not been played yet. It is not an object
with only null fields: the client needs to know whether statistics exist at
all before it renders a section for them.
MatchDetail.title: MatchDetail

MatchOdds.description:
The pre-closing 1x2 price of the fixture and the probabilities it implies.

``bookmaker`` is the source of the row, selected by the loader's bookmaker
priority, and ``is_closing`` is literally false: a closing price is only
known at kickoff, so serving one would describe the fixture with information
nobody could have had earlier. The three prices are the stored decimals as
floats, in ``home``/``draw``/``away`` order.

``implied`` is derived from exactly these three prices by removing the
bookmaker's margin proportionally, so its values sum to one and are not
stored anywhere. It is a forecast of the market, not of a model, which is
why it is a separate object from ``predictions``.
MatchOdds.title: MatchOdds

MatchPage.description:
One page of fixtures.

The generic envelope is specialised here so the generated client and the
OpenAPI document name a concrete schema, ``MatchPage``, instead of an
anonymous generic.
MatchPage.title: MatchPage

MatchPreview.description:
Everything the preview of one fixture serves.

``match`` is the fixture itself, nested rather than referenced, so a client
renders the clubs, the date and the status from one response. ``home_form``
and ``away_form`` are the recent form of both sides, read strictly before
the fixture's kickoff date. ``head_to_head`` is the record of the pair and
its ten most recent meetings. ``predictions`` holds the standing stored
forecast of every model of the fixture, whatever its evaluation. ``odds`` is
the pre-closing price of the fixture or null when it carries none.

Two preview items this resource deliberately does not carry: the
opponent's profile beyond the form of both sides, and how much the result
moves the relegation probability. Both need an input or a core rule this
resource does not own, not another field here.
MatchPreview.title: MatchPreview

MatchStats.description:
The per-team statistics of one match.

One field per source column, so a client renders what is stored without
guessing. The expected goals are floats: the database keeps them as a
decimal with two places, but a client computes with them, and a decimal
serialised as a string would force it to parse them first.
MatchStats.title: MatchStats

MatchSummary.description:
One fixture as a collection returns it.

``season`` is the season code, not its identifier, because that is the code
a client passes back as a filter. The two teams are nested objects rather
than identifiers: a list of fixtures is rendered with the club names, and
nesting them costs nothing because the endpoint reads them from the same
query. ``kickoff_time`` is ``None`` when the source did not publish a time.
MatchSummary.title: MatchSummary

MetricRow.description:
The metrics of one model on one season or on all scored seasons.

``season_code`` is ``seasons.code``; ``None`` is the overall row.
``coverage`` is ``n_matches / n_fixtures``; ``load_report`` computes it, so
a stored row does not carry it.
MetricRow.title: MetricRow

MetricScores.description:
The aggregate scores of one model on one match set.

The scores are computed over the same matched rows, so ``n_matches`` is the
single count a reader needs to judge how much the numbers mean.

brier.description: Mean Brier score over the scored matches.
brier.title: Brier

log_loss.description: Mean log loss over the scored matches.
log_loss.title: Log Loss

MetricScores.title: MetricScores

ModelInfo.description:
One model of a run, as ``describe()`` reports it.

The hyperparameters are recorded next to the metrics so a reader can tell
which settings produced them. ``version`` is bumped whenever a
hyperparameter or the math changes.
ModelInfo.title: ModelInfo

ModelMetrics.description:
The live metrics of one model and one version.

The version is part of the identity because two rows of a model with
different versions are not comparable and must not be pooled.

model_version.description: The model version the rows were produced by.
model_version.title: Model Version

scores.description: The aggregate scores of this model.

ModelMetrics.title: ModelMetrics

ModelMetricsResponse.description:
One backtest run and its results, ordered per the API contract.

The lists are ordered by the producer: models in :data:`BACKTEST_MODEL_NAMES`
order, metrics by season and then ``all`` before ``common``, and
calibration by model, outcome and bin index.
ModelMetricsResponse.title: ModelMetricsResponse

NextMatch.description:
The club's next fixture and the projection of each of its outcomes.

``match_id`` names the fixture the outcomes belong to, so a client links to
the match endpoint without matching on a date, and the outcomes nest under
it so one response carries both. ``current`` is the club's row of the same
run, so every outcome is compared against the baseline the run measured
rather than against a second simulation.

The block comes from the latest succeeded run of the season and is null when
that run did not store it: a run created before revision 0004 has no
next-match detail, a stored match that is no longer the club's next fixture
is answered as unknown by
:func:`lmi_core.analytics.relegation.next_match_swing`, a result the run never
sampled has no conditional probability, and a run without a row for the club
has no ``current`` to compare against.
NextMatch.title: NextMatch

NextMatchCurrent.description:
The club's own row of the same run the next-match swing comes from.

``p_relegation``, ``p_europe`` and ``p_title`` are the run's probabilities for
the club over the whole remaining season, and ``expected_points`` is its
expected final total -- the value ``rivals[].expected_points`` already
carries. Reading these four numbers and the swing from one run is what lets a
client compute every delta of the block against one consistent baseline
instead of mixing two runs' projections.
NextMatchCurrent.title: NextMatchCurrent

NextMatchOutcome.description:
What one outcome of the next match would do to the club's projected season.

The four probabilities and the expected total are what the latest succeeded
run of the season measured for that outcome, so a client compares a win, a
draw and a loss on one scale instead of reading one projected table.
``p_outcome`` is the share of the simulated runs that produced the outcome,
while ``p_relegation``, ``p_europe`` and ``p_title`` are the shares of those
same runs that ended each way; ``expected_points`` is their mean final total.
Because ``p_outcome`` is a sampled frequency, it may differ slightly -- about
half a percentage point at 10 000 runs -- from the model probability the same
run stores for the fixture.
NextMatchOutcome.title: NextMatchOutcome

NextMatchOutcomes.description:
The three outcomes of the next match, each with its projection.

Every outcome is present, because the value of the block is the comparison:
a client that lacks one of the three cannot say what a draw would cost.
NextMatchOutcomes.title: NextMatchOutcomes

PerMatch.description:
The team's own and its opponents' per-match averages over the season.

``for_`` is the team's line and ``against`` the line of the clubs it faced.
The two are kept apart so a team that wins without creating chances is
distinguishable from one that creates without winning. The JSON key of the
first side is ``for``, which is why the attribute is ``for_``.
PerMatch.title: PerMatch

PredictionBrief.description:
One prediction as the team focus and the match preview nest it.

The shape is the part of :class:`PredictionOut` those two resources need:
the identity a client follows to the detail endpoint, the model that
produced the forecast, the moment and the as-of date, the probabilities and
the evaluation. The match is deliberately absent, because both resources
nest the brief inside the fixture it belongs to.
PredictionBrief.title: PredictionBrief

PredictionCounts.description:
The per-outcome counts of the evaluated prediction rows.

The counts explain which subset the metrics cover: only ``scored`` rows have
scores, and the remaining rows are the reason a model's coverage is below
one.

n_late.description: Rows stored at or after the match date.
n_late.title: N Late

n_pending.description: Rows whose match has not been played.
n_pending.title: N Pending

n_scored.description: Rows with a result and an on-time prediction.
n_scored.title: N Scored

n_superseded.description: Rows replaced by a later as-of date.
n_superseded.title: N Superseded

PredictionCounts.title: PredictionCounts

PredictionDetail.description:
One stored prediction with the run that wrote it and its configuration.

``run_id`` is the prediction run the row belongs to, and ``model_config`` is
the configuration the model recorded at write time, so a reader can tell
which settings produced the probabilities without a second request. The
attribute is named ``config`` because pydantic reserves ``model_config`` for
the configuration of the model class itself; the payload key is the
documented ``model_config``, which the field carries as its alias.
PredictionDetail.title: PredictionDetail

PredictionOut.description:
One stored prediction of one match and model.

``match`` is the fixture the prediction is for, nested rather than
referenced, because a client renders the club names and the kickoff date
next to the probabilities and the endpoint reads them from the same request.
``as_of_date`` is the Madrid date the prediction was produced for and
``created_at`` the instant the database stored it: the two differ, and the
evaluation depends on the second.

``odds_source`` names the bookmaker the forecast priced the match with, and
is null when the match carried no eligible price. ``score`` is filled only
for a ``scored`` row, so a client reads ``evaluation`` first and treats
``score`` as its consequence.
PredictionOut.title: PredictionOut

PredictionPage.description:
One page of stored predictions.

The generic envelope is specialised here so the generated client and the
OpenAPI document name a concrete schema, ``PredictionPage``, instead of an
anonymous generic.
PredictionPage.title: PredictionPage

PredictionScore.description:
The four scores of one on-time prediction of a played match.

``log_loss``, ``brier`` and ``rps`` are the backtest metric functions on this one
row, and ``correct`` says whether the most likely outcome is the one that
happened. The values are null-free because the object exists only for a
scored row: an absent score is a null field on the parent, never an object
with null numbers.
PredictionScore.title: PredictionScore

Probabilities.description:
The probability triple of one stored prediction.

The three values are the stored columns, in the order the models emit them,
and they sum to one within the tolerance the database check enforces. They
are not renormalised on read: a served probability is exactly the number the
worker stored.
Probabilities.title: Probabilities

Problem.description:
An RFC 9457 problem details body.

``type`` is ``"about:blank"`` because the API does not publish problem type
URIs: the HTTP status and the ``title`` carry the meaning. ``errors`` is set
only by a validation failure; ``detail`` is ``None`` for an internal error,
whose cause stays in the server log.
Problem.title: Problem

RelegationRace.description:
One club's relegation race in one season.

``survival_threshold`` is the historical survival line the club is measured
against, ``rivals`` the club and the nearest clubs of the latest succeeded
simulation, ``series`` the run history of exactly those clubs, and
``remaining_fixtures`` the club's fixtures still to play. ``run_id`` and
``as_of_date`` name the simulation the rivals and the series come from and
are null when the season has none.

``next_match`` is the club's next fixture with what each of its results does
to the race, read from the same run as the rivals and the series. It is null
when that run stored no next-match detail for the club, or answered unknown
for it: an absent block says the run did not measure it, not that the club
has no fixture left.
RelegationRace.title: RelegationRace

RelegationRival.description:
One club of the race, with the stored numbers the group compares.

``team`` is the club, ``current_points`` its real total at the run's as-of
date, and the rest are the run's projection of it: the mean final total, the
relegation probability and the low and high ends of the projected total.
Every number is a stored column of that one run, so no value here is
re-simulated or recomputed on read.
RelegationRival.title: RelegationRival

RemainingFixture.description:
One fixture the club still has to play, with what is known about it.

``venue`` is where the club plays it, and ``opponent_position`` the
opponent's place in the season's table, or null for a club the table does
not rank. ``p_win``, ``p_draw`` and ``p_loss`` are the run's probabilities of
the three results from the club's side: at home the stored ``p_home``,
``p_draw`` and ``p_away``, away the same triple read from the other end, so
``p_win`` always describes the club and not the venue. They come from the
latest succeeded run of the season and are null when that run did not store
the fixture, which is the case for a run created before revision 0004 and for
a fixture the run did not simulate.
RemainingFixture.title: RemainingFixture

Rolling5.description:
Averages over the at most five matches immediately before one match.

The window never includes the match it describes, so the line answers what
the team did before kickoff. Every field is null when the window is empty,
which is the team's first match of the season.
Rolling5.title: Rolling5

Season.description:
One league season as the API returns it.

Only the two fields a client sorts or displays are exposed. ``code`` is the
human-readable identifier, for example ``2025-26``, and ``start_year`` is
the calendar year the season began in, which orders the seasons.
Season.title: Season

SeasonMatchLine.description:
One played match of the season, seen from the team's side.

``match`` is the fixture summary, nested so a client renders the clubs, the
date and the score without a second request. ``shots_for`` and
``shots_against`` are the shots columns only, and are null when that side of
the match has no statistics row or no shots value.
SeasonMatchLine.title: SeasonMatchLine

SeasonTiers.description:
The team's season split by the tier of the opponent it faced.

With ``n`` teams in the season the top tier is positions ``1..ceil(n/3)``,
the middle the next ``ceil(n/3)`` and the bottom the rest, so the three
records partition the table exactly. A table of fewer than five clubs can
leave the bottom tier empty -- with ``n = 4``, ``ceil(n/3) = 2`` fills the
top and the middle and leaves nothing for the bottom -- and an empty tier is
served as a record of zeros with a null ``points_per_game`` and an empty
``team_ids`` rather than being dropped.
SeasonTiers.title: SeasonTiers

SimulationCurrent.description:
The real standing of one team at the run's as-of date.

These are the played matches the run counted as fixed results, so a client
compares the current column with the projected one on the same scale.
SimulationCurrent.title: SimulationCurrent

SimulationDetail.description:
One run with the table it projected.

``table`` is in projected table order: mean final position ascending, then
mean points descending, then the club name and its identifier. It is empty
unless ``run.status`` is ``succeeded``, because a run that has not executed
has written no team rows; an empty table is therefore never a claim that the
league has no teams.
SimulationDetail.title: SimulationDetail

SimulationHistory.description:
The forecast history of one season, one point per as-of date.

``points`` ascends by ``as_of_date``, so a client draws the series in the
order the season happened. A date contributes one point, and a date the
simulator never succeeded on contributes none: the history is the record of
stored answers and not a calendar.
SimulationHistory.title: SimulationHistory

SimulationHistoryPoint.description:
The forecast of one as-of date.

``run_id`` names the run the numbers come from: the latest succeeded run of
that date, so a date that was simulated more than once yields its last
answer and not an average of several. ``kind`` tells a live forecast from a
retroactive one, because a backfilled date answers "what would the season
have looked like then", not "what did we say then".

``teams`` is in projected table order, filtered to the caller's team when it
asked for one. A team that a run does not mention is absent from the point
rather than present with zero probabilities.
SimulationHistoryPoint.title: SimulationHistoryPoint

SimulationHistoryTeam.description:
One team in one point of the history.

Only the summary of the team's projected season is kept: the history exists
to show how a forecast moved from matchday to matchday, so it carries the
small set of numbers that can be compared across dates. The full row of a
single run is :class:`SimulationTeamRow`, served by the detail endpoint.
SimulationHistoryTeam.title: SimulationHistoryTeam

SimulationOutlook.description:
One team's row in the latest succeeded simulation of the season.

Every number is a stored column of that run: the four qualification
probabilities, ``expected_points`` (the stored ``mean_points``),
``expected_position`` (the stored ``mean_position``) and the two stored
points quantiles. Nothing is re-simulated and nothing is recomputed on read,
so the outlook of a run never changes after the run finished, and the
``run_id`` is the trace back to the full table of that run.

``points_p05`` and ``points_p95`` are the 5th and 95th percentile of the
simulated final points total, which is why they are whole points while the
expected values are not.
SimulationOutlook.title: SimulationOutlook

SimulationPointsDistribution.description:
The full distribution of one team's final points total.

``min`` is the lowest total the run reached, which is the value the first
entry of ``probabilities`` belongs to: entry ``i`` is the probability of
finishing on ``min + i`` points, so the array covers every total between its
ends and no gap. The entries sum to one within floating-point tolerance.
SimulationPointsDistribution.title: SimulationPointsDistribution

SimulationPointsQuantiles.description:
The quantiles of one team's final points total.

Each value is a total the run reached, not an offset, so it is directly
comparable with ``current.points`` and ``expected_points``.
SimulationPointsQuantiles.title: SimulationPointsQuantiles

SimulationQualification.description:
Where the continental and relegation places of the run start.

``ucl_positions`` and ``europe_positions`` count places from the top, so a
team qualifies when its final position is at most that number;
``relegation_positions`` counts places from the bottom. The thresholds are
stored with the run, because a change of the competition format must not
rewrite what a past run meant.
SimulationQualification.title: SimulationQualification

SimulationRequest.description:
What a client asks the simulator to run.

Every field is optional: the season defaults to the one the season endpoints
open on, the as-of date defaults to the Madrid date, the run count to
:data:`DEFAULT_N_RUNS` and the seed to :data:`DEFAULT_SEED`.

``as_of_date`` is the last date whose played matches count as fixed results.
The endpoint refuses a date later than the Madrid date, because a simulation
of matches whose results are not known yet would be a forecast dressed as a
table. ``n_runs`` and ``seed`` carry their bounds on the fields, so a value
outside them is a validation failure of the whole API and never reaches the
endpoint.
SimulationRequest.title: SimulationRequest

SimulationRun.description:
One stored simulation request.

``season`` is the code of the season the run simulates, spelled the way the
season endpoints spell it, and ``as_of_date`` is the last date whose played
matches the run may count as fixed. ``n_runs`` and ``seed`` are the size and
the seed of the Monte Carlo draw, and together with the season, the as-of
date and the model they are the run's natural key while it is active.

``qualification`` repeats the thresholds the run was requested with, so a
client reads the meaning of ``p_ucl``, ``p_europe`` and ``p_relegation``
from the same payload instead of assuming today's competition format.
SimulationRun.title: SimulationRun

SimulationRunPage.description:
One page of stored runs, most recently requested first.

The generic envelope is specialised here so the generated client and the
OpenAPI document name a concrete schema, ``SimulationRunPage``, instead of an
anonymous generic.
SimulationRunPage.title: SimulationRunPage

SimulationTeamRow.description:
One team of a run's projected table.

``team`` is the club, ``current`` its real standing at the as-of date and the
rest is what the simulation says about it. ``expected_points`` is the mean
final total and ``expected_position`` the mean final position, which is not
necessarily an integer and is not the position of the row in the table.

``position_probabilities`` has one entry per team of the league: index
``i`` is the probability of finishing at position ``i + 1``, so index 0 is
first place. It therefore sums to one, like ``points_distribution``.
SimulationTeamRow.title: SimulationTeamRow

SplitRecord.description:
The counters of one group of matches seen from one team's side.

The record is used for the home and the away half of a season, so every
number covers only the matches of that group. ``points_per_game`` is
``points / played`` and is null, never ``0.0``, when the group is empty: a
side that has not played a match has no average, and a zero would read as a
side that played and earned nothing.
SplitRecord.title: SplitRecord

StandingRow.description:
One team's line in the table.

Every counter covers only the matches the response counted: the played
matches of the season up to ``as_of``, or all of them when ``as_of`` is
absent. A team whose fixtures have not been played yet keeps its row, with
every counter at zero and an empty ``form``, so the table always lists the
whole season and never hides a club that has not started.

``goal_difference`` is ``goals_for - goals_against`` and may be negative.
``form`` holds at most the five most recent outcomes, most recent first,
which is why it can be shorter than ``played``.
StandingRow.title: StandingRow

Standings.description:
The table of one season, with the scope it was computed for.

``season`` is the season code, which is also what a client passes back as
the ``season`` filter of the other endpoints. ``as_of`` repeats the cutoff
the request asked for and is ``None`` when the table counts every played
match of the season. ``matches_counted`` is the number of results that went
into the counters, so a client can tell an empty table from a table whose
matchdays have not been played yet.

``rows`` is ordered as the competition ranks it, positions ``1..n`` with no
shared place. The API does not re-sort it.
Standings.title: Standings

StatLine.description:
A per-match average line of one side, every field optional.

``goals`` is averaged over every counted match; each other field is averaged
over only the matches that carry it, so the denominators can differ by
field. A null field means the counted matches hold no value for it, which a
client renders as unknown.
StatLine.title: StatLine

SurvivalThreshold.description:
The historical survival line of the league, as the payload serves it.

``points_median`` is the median final total of the counted place over the
counted seasons and is never rounded, while ``points_min`` and
``points_max`` are the extremes of the same sample. ``seasons_used`` makes
the sample size visible, so a median of one season is not read as a median
of ten, and ``position`` names the place the sample was read from.
SurvivalThreshold.title: SurvivalThreshold

Team.description:
One club as the API returns it.

``id`` is the stable identifier a client uses to link to a team; ``name`` is
the canonical spelling stored in the database, not a source-specific alias.
Team.title: Team

TeamFocus.description:
Everything one team's focus view serves about one season.

``season`` is the season code the other endpoints accept as their filter.
``standing`` is the team's row of the season table, ``form`` its last five
played matches of the season and ``splits`` all of them by venue, so the
three describe the same matches from three angles. ``upcoming`` are the next
fixtures of the season with the forecasts stored for them, and ``outlook``
is the simulated season of the latest succeeded run.

The scope is deliberately the season: a form string that mixed seasons would
compare a team's August with its May of another year.
TeamFocus.title: TeamFocus

TeamHistory.description:
A club's seasons, ascending, and the steepest decline of each metric.

``seasons`` lists only the seasons the club played, so a season it did not
play is absent rather than a line of zeros; a club with no played match has
an empty list. ``largest_drop`` is empty when nothing declined and when
fewer than two seasons are listed. Both the order and the emptiness rules
are :mod:`lmi_core.analytics.history`'s.
TeamHistory.title: TeamHistory

TeamHistoryDrop.description:
The steepest decline of one metric between two adjacent seasons.

``metric`` is the payload key of the number the entry describes: one of
``points_pg``, ``goals_for_pg``, ``goals_against_pg``, ``shots_for_pg``,
``shots_against_pg``, ``sot_for_pg``, ``sot_against_pg``, ``cards_pg`` and
``xpts_pg``. It stays a plain string because that list is the rule of
:mod:`lmi_core.analytics.history`; a second copy here would be free to drift
from it.

``delta`` is negative and oriented so it always means the club got worse.
``from_season`` is the earlier season and ``to_season`` the later, both taken
from the history order. A pair with a missing value on either side is
skipped for that metric, because a gap in the source is not a fall to zero.
TeamHistoryDrop.title: TeamHistoryDrop

TeamHistorySeason.description:
One season of a club's history, with its table position and per-game averages.

``position`` is the club's place in that season's table, ``None`` when the
table holds no row for it. ``played``, ``points``, ``points_pg``,
``goals_for_pg`` and ``goals_against_pg`` are always known for a listed
season; every other average is ``None`` when no counted match of that season
carries the value, and is averaged over only the matches that do. Those
denominators and the null-is-never-zero rule belong to
:mod:`lmi_core.analytics.history`.
TeamHistorySeason.title: TeamHistorySeason

TeamSeasonStats.description:
Everything one team's season serves: averages, tiers and one row per match.

``season`` is the season code the other endpoints accept as their filter.
``played`` and ``points`` are the table's counters over the same played
matches, ``per_match`` and ``league_avg`` are the season's own and the
league-wide per-match averages, and the coverage counters say how many
matches each derived number rests on. ``splits`` covers the season by venue
and ``tiers`` by the opponent's table position, while ``matches`` is the
chronological season the rolling form of each row is computed from.
TeamSeasonStats.title: TeamSeasonStats

TeamSplits.description:
The season of one team split by venue.

``home`` counts the matches the team played as the home side and ``away``
the ones it played as the visitor. The two records are kept apart because
home advantage is real enough that a pooled number hides the side that is
failing.
TeamSplits.title: TeamSplits

TierRecord.description:
The record of a team's matches against one tier of the season table.

The counters are the same shape as a venue split and cover every match
against a club of that tier, whatever the venue. ``team_ids`` is the
membership of the tier, ascending: the clubs that occupy those table
positions, not only the opponents this team has already met.
TierRecord.title: TierRecord

UpcomingMatch.description:
One fixture still to be played, with the stored forecasts of it.

``predictions`` holds one brief per model and is empty when no model has a
stored forecast for the fixture yet, which is the normal state of a match
several days out. The fixture is nested rather than referenced so a client
renders the clubs, the date and the probabilities from one response.
UpcomingMatch.title: UpcomingMatch

VersionResponse.description: Build identity of the running service.
VersionResponse.title: VersionResponse

info.description: La Liga Match Intelligence: the only entry point to LMI data.
info.title: LMI API

get.description: Report that the service is up.

Return one page of recorded runs, most recently started first.

Every filter is optional and the ones given are combined with ``AND``: a
data source, a season code and a run status. ``source`` and ``status`` are
literals, so a value outside the two sources or the three statuses is
rejected by the request validation and never reaches this function.

``total`` is the number of runs the filter matched in the whole table, not
the size of ``items``, so a client renders a result count and asks for the
next page without a second call. ``limit`` and ``offset`` are echoed from
the request.

The order is the start instant descending, with the identifier descending as
a tie-break: two runs that started in the same instant then still have one
order, so paging the same filter twice cannot move a row between pages.

The season filter is probed against the ``seasons`` table before the page is
read. The run table keeps the code as plain text, so a code no season has
would otherwise be a valid filter value that merely matched no row, and the
answer would depend on whether some run happens to carry that code.

The route path is empty on purpose: the router prefix is the whole path, so
``GET /v1/ingestion-runs`` is served directly instead of redirecting from
``/v1/ingestion-runs/``. The return annotation is the response model, so no
``response_model`` is passed.

The request issues three statements: the season probe when a season code is
given, one count and one page. The page statement selects the whole run row
and the payload is built from it field by field, because the models declare
no relationship the code could lazy-load per row.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when ``season`` names no stored season. The detail is
        a fixed sentence and never repeats the value the client sent.

Return one recorded run with the source rows it rejected.

The rejections are the first ``REJECTION_PAGE_SIZE`` of the run in
``row_number`` order, with the identifier as the tie-break, and
``rejections_total`` is the count of every rejection of the run. A client
therefore knows whether the embedded list is complete, and no rejection
costs a second statement: the count and the page are one statement each,
whatever the size of the run.

The return annotation is the response model, so no ``response_model`` is
passed. The payload of the run itself is the one the collection returns,
built by the same function, and the rejections are appended to it.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no stored run has ``run_id``. The detail is a
        fixed sentence and never repeats the identifier.

Return one page of fixtures, most chronological first by default.

Every filter is optional and the ones given are combined with ``AND``: a
season code, a team that played home or away, a matchday, a status, and an
inclusive range of kickoff dates. The two dates are compared on
``kickoff_date`` only, so a range covers whole days and a match without a
kickoff time is still in it.

``total`` is the number of fixtures the filter matched in the whole
database, not the size of ``items``, so a client renders a result count and
asks for the next page without a second call.

The sort key is the kickoff date, then the kickoff time, then the
identifier. A fixture whose source published no time therefore never jumps
to the top of its day and never leads the list in reverse: the null time
sorts last in both directions, while the date and the identifier still
reverse. Within one day ``desc`` reverses the relative order of the timed
fixtures and still ends with the untimed ones, so the two orders agree on a
day that holds one timed fixture and diverge once a day holds two.

The request path issues two statements, one for the count and one for the
page, whatever the size of the page: both teams come from explicit joins on
the same statement, because the models declare no relationship the code
could lazy-load per row. The only exception is a page that matched nothing
while a season code or a team identifier was given: one existence probe per
value given, so at most two, decides between an empty page and a 404. The
probes run after the count and before the page statement, because a miss is
only possible when the count is zero: an unknown value raises there, a known
one falls through to the page query.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when ``season`` or ``team_id`` names no stored row.
        The detail is a fixed sentence and never repeats the value, so the
        response says which kind of thing is unknown and nothing more.
    RequestValidationError: 422 when ``date_from`` is after ``date_to``,
        rendered by the installed handler as a problem details body that
        names the offending parameter and not the dates.

Return one fixture with its statistics.

The statistics row is fetched by an outer join on the same statement, so a
match without statistics is one statement with a null row and not a second
request.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no stored match has ``match_id``. The detail is
        a fixed sentence and never repeats the identifier.

Return the pre-kickoff view of one fixture.

``match`` is the fixture itself, read through the shared match reader so the
payload names the clubs, the season and the date the same way every other
match resource does.

``home_form`` and ``away_form`` are the form of each side over the played
matches dated strictly before the fixture's own kickoff date, five at most
and across seasons. The bound is the leakage rule: the fixture itself, a
fixture of the same day and every later one are excluded, so the form is the
one a reader could have seen before kickoff, and a played match's preview
shows the form it had then rather than the form it has now.

``head_to_head`` is the same rule applied to the pair. A league pair meets
twice a season, so the full prior set is read and counted -- truncating the
read would silently change ``played`` -- and only the payload list is capped
at the ten most recent meetings. The three counters are seen from *this*
fixture's home team, not from the venue of each earlier meeting, so the club
that was the visitor in a prior meeting still counts its own wins.

``predictions`` holds the standing stored forecast of every model of the
fixture, whatever it earned: a played match yields ``scored`` briefs, a
scheduled one ``pending``, a withdrawn one ``withdrawn`` and a fixture whose
date moved earlier than its rows ``late``. The evaluation is the core
scorer's, so this resource cannot disagree with ``/v1/predictions`` or
``/v1/model-metrics/live``.

``odds`` is the pre-closing 1x2 price of the fixture, selected by the
bookmaker priority the live loader uses, and null when the fixture carries
no eligible price -- the normal state of a match still to be played, since
the current sources publish odds only with results. No price is invented and
no closing price is served.

Two preview items this resource deliberately does not carry: the
opponent's profile beyond the form of both sides, and how much the result
moves the relegation probability. Both need an input or a core rule this
resource does not own, not another field here.

The request issues at most nine statements whatever the size of the payload:
one for the fixture, two for each of the two form summaries, two for the
head-to-head read, one for the stored predictions and one for the price. A
read that matched nothing issues fewer, never more.

The return annotation is the response model, so no ``response_model`` is
passed.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no stored match has ``match_id``. The detail is
        a fixed sentence and never repeats the identifier.

Return the stored report of one backtest run, or of the latest one.

The resource is the whole result of a walk-forward backtest: the run header,
the models it scored, their metrics and their calibration bins. ``run_id``
selects a stored run; without it the latest succeeded run is served, which
is the one a dashboard opens on. The report is returned as the store orders
it, so the API adds no second definition of the contract order.

Only a succeeded run is served. :func:`~lmi_core.results.store.load_report`
returns ``None`` both when no succeeded run is stored and when ``run_id``
names a run that is missing, still ``running`` or ``failed``, so every miss
is the same 404 and the response never discloses which ids are in flight.

The route path is empty on purpose: the router prefix is the whole path, so
``GET /v1/model-metrics`` is served directly instead of redirecting from
``/v1/model-metrics/``. The return annotation is the response model, so no
``response_model`` is passed. A malformed ``run_id`` is rejected by the
query validation and rendered by the installed handler, so only the 404 is
raised here.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no succeeded run matches the request.

Return the live metrics of one season, derived from the stored rows.

Every number comes from :func:`lmi_core.live.scoring.live_metrics`, which is
the same function the worker's ``predict --report`` prints through. This
module only selects the rows it is given, so the endpoint and the worker
cannot disagree about an outcome, a score or a count.

``season`` selects the matches whose predictions are scored. Without it the
season that starts latest among the seasons with a match is served, exactly
as the standings endpoint selects it, so both resources open on the season
ingestion has loaded. The season bounds the match identifiers read, not the
predictions table: a request for one season never scores another season's
rows.

``market_reference`` is recomputed from the pre-closing 1x2 odds of the
played matches, through the loader's bookmaker priority and margin removal. The
prices are pre-kickoff information, but they were not stored as a live row,
which is why the reference always reports ``stored_before_kickoff`` false
and is a benchmark rather than a stored prediction.

The report's ``evaluated_as_of`` is the Madrid date of the request, read
from :func:`lmi_core.clock.madrid_today`, which is the same source the
worker's publisher uses, so the two reports name the same evaluation day.

``season`` is a free string and rejects no value before the lookup, so the
only error this route raises is the 404 of an unknown code; the shared
problem responses still declare the 422 a query validation could produce.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when ``season`` is given and no season has that code,
        or when no season has a match while ``season`` is absent. The detail
        is a fixed sentence and never repeats the client value.

Return one page of stored predictions with the outcome each one earned.

Every filter is optional and the ones given are combined with ``AND``. A
season code selects that season; without one the season that starts latest
among the seasons with a match is served, exactly as the standings endpoint
selects it. ``match_id`` restricts the page to one fixture and ``team_id``
to the fixtures a team played home or away, ``matchday`` to the fixtures of
one matchday of the season, ``model`` to one registered model name,
``match_status`` to the current status of the match, and the two dates to an
inclusive range of ``kickoff_date``, so a range covers whole days.

The two derived filters are ordered, and the order is part of the contract.
``latest_only`` projects the rows the *other* filters selected onto one
standing row per ``(match, model)``, and ``evaluation`` then restricts that
projection. So ``evaluation=superseded`` with ``latest_only=true`` is
normally empty, because a superseded row never stands for its group, while
``latest_only=false`` is the whole ledger the other filters selected and
returns every superseded row. The default answers the question a dashboard
asks, one forecast per match and model; ``latest_only=false`` answers what
the worker stored.

``total`` is the number of rows the filters matched before the page was
sliced, not the size of ``items``, so a client renders a result count and
asks for the next page without a second call. The order is the kickoff date
ascending, then the match identifier, then the model in the registry order
and then the as-of date descending: a match with two models lists them in
report order, and the ledger of one model lists its newest row first.

The request issues a fixed number of statements whatever the size of the
page: the season resolution, at most one existence probe per filter value
given, one statement for the match identifiers of the season, one for the
stored predictions and one for the match summaries of the page. The
summaries cover the rows on the page only, so the response does not read the
fixture of every match the filters matched.

The route path is empty on purpose: the router prefix is the whole path, so
``GET /v1/predictions`` is served directly instead of redirecting from
``/v1/predictions/``. The return annotation is the response model, so no
``response_model`` is passed.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when ``season`` names no stored season, or when
        ``match_id`` or ``team_id`` names no stored row. The detail is a
        fixed sentence in every case and never repeats the value the client
        sent.
    RequestValidationError: 422 when ``date_from`` is after ``date_to``, or
        when ``matchday`` is outside ``1..46``, rendered by the installed
        handler as a problem details body that names the offending
        parameter and not the values.

Return one stored prediction with the run that wrote it.

The stored row is read by identifier, and then every stored prediction of
the same match is read and evaluated, so the served ``evaluation`` and
``score`` are the group-correct ones: a row that a later as-of date replaced
is ``superseded`` even when its match already has a result, which is exactly
what the collection reports for it. Scoring the single row on its own would
call it ``scored`` and disagree with the ledger the collection serves.

The detail adds the two columns the collection drops: ``run_id``, the
prediction run of the row, and ``model_config``, the configuration the model
recorded at write time. The payload is built through ``model_validate``
because the configuration field carries the documented ``model_config`` as
its alias: pydantic reserves that attribute name for the model class
configuration.

The return annotation is the response model, so no ``response_model`` is
passed.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no stored prediction has ``prediction_id``. The
        detail is a fixed sentence and never repeats the identifier.

Return every stored season, most recent first.

Ordering by ``start_year`` descending puts the current season first, which
is the one a dashboard opens on.

The route path is empty on purpose: the router prefix is the whole path, so
``GET /v1/seasons`` is served directly instead of redirecting from
``/v1/seasons/``. The return annotation is the response model and the
endpoint has no error path, so neither ``response_model`` nor ``responses``
is passed.

Return one page of stored runs, most recently requested first.

The filters are combined with ``AND`` and all are optional. ``status`` and
``kind`` are literals, so a value outside the four states or the two kinds is
refused by the request validation and never reaches this function. ``season``
is probed against the ``seasons`` table first, so an unknown code is a 404
instead of a page that merely came back empty.

An omitted ``season`` selects the season that starts latest among the seasons
with at least one run, so a dashboard opens on the season somebody has
actually simulated. When no season has a run the answer is an empty page with
status 200, not a 404: the collection exists, it is simply empty.

``total`` is the number of runs the filters matched in the whole table, not
the size of ``items``, so a client renders a result count and asks for the
next page without a second call. The order is the request instant descending
with the identifier descending as a tie-break, so two runs requested in the
same instant still have one order and paging the same filter twice cannot
move a row between pages.

The request issues at most three statements: the season probe, one count and
one page, and the page statement joins the season explicitly because the
models declare no relationship the payload could lazy-load per row.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when ``season`` names no stored season. The detail is
        a fixed sentence and never repeats the value the client sent.

post.description:
Ask for a simulation run, store it and hand it to the worker.

The answer is 202 and not 201: the row is stored, but nothing has been
simulated yet, and ``run.status`` is ``queued`` until a worker claims it. The
identifier in the ``Location`` header is where the client polls, and the body
describes the row exactly as it was stored.

An omitted ``season`` selects the season that starts latest among the seasons
with at least one match, which is the season the standings endpoint opens on.
An omitted ``as_of_date`` is the Madrid date. An ``as_of_date`` later than
that date is refused before any row is written: the run would count matches
whose results nobody knows as if they had been played.

A request identical to an active run does not create a second one. The
natural key of an active run is the season, the as-of date, the run count,
the seed and the model, so the same body twice answers the identifier the
first request produced, with no second message to the worker. The runs that
already exist and are alive therefore stay the single truth about what has
been asked for.

The row is committed before the message is sent, so the worker that receives
the identifier always finds the row it names. When the queue refuses the
message and the run is still ``queued``, the run cannot execute, so it is
marked ``failed`` with the enqueue instant as its start and finish, and the
request answers 503: a run left ``queued`` would look alive to a client that
polls it and to every later identical request, which would then be told to
wait for work nobody is doing. A queued row that is merely stale is instead
re-enqueued by the next identical request, which is why the failure is
recorded rather than retried here.

A message that did reach the broker can be claimed before the enqueue call
reports its error. Such a claim is not overwritten: the worker owns the run
and is executing it, so the answer is the ordinary 202 that describes the
stored row instead of a failure, and the client polls the real state.

Args:
    body: the season, as-of date, size and seed the client asked for.
    session: the session that inserts the run and records a failure.
    queue: the producer that hands the committed identifier to the worker.
    response: the response whose ``Location`` header names the new run.

Returns:
    The stored run, as it looks after the operation.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 422 when ``as_of_date`` is later than the Madrid date, 404
        when the season names no stored season or no season has a match
        while the body names none, and 503 when the queue refused the
        message and the run was recorded as failed.

get.description:
Return one forecast point per as-of date of a season, ascending.

A date contributes the latest succeeded run of that date and nothing else:
when a day was requested twice and both attempts succeeded, the answer is the
one that finished last, so the history is the series of final answers and not
a series of attempts. A date without a succeeded run contributes no point, so
the series is a record of forecasts and not a calendar.

``team_id`` narrows every point to one club, keeping the other columns of the
point: a client tracks how one team's projected season moved from matchday to
matchday. A date whose run does not mention the club keeps its point with an
empty ``teams`` list, because the point is a stored forecast and dropping it
would silently shorten the season.

An omitted ``season`` selects the season that starts latest among the seasons
with at least one run, the rule the collection and ``latest`` follow. A
stored season without a run answers an empty history; a body that names no
season while no season has a run is a 404, because the empty answer would
otherwise describe a season the request never selected.

The request issues at most four statements: the season probe, the team probe
when a club is given, one statement for the runs and one for their team rows,
whatever the number of points. Both joins are explicit, because the models
declare no relationship.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when ``season`` names no stored season, when
        ``team_id`` names no stored team, or when neither is given and no
        season has a run. The details are fixed sentences.

Return the most recent succeeded run of a season with its projected table.

"Most recent" is the finish instant descending, with the request instant and
the identifier as tie-breaks, so the answer is the last forecast the season
produced rather than the last one somebody asked for: a run still queued, or
one that failed, is not an answer a dashboard can draw.

An omitted ``season`` selects the season that starts latest among the seasons
with at least one run, the same rule the collection uses, so the two views
agree on which season a client is looking at. A season whose runs all failed
is a 404 and not an empty table: "no succeeded simulation" is a state of the
season, not a table with no rows.

The path is declared before ``/{run_id}`` so that ``latest`` is never read as
a run identifier. The body is the shape of the single-run request, built by
the same helpers, so the two endpoints cannot drift apart.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when ``season`` names no stored season, or when the
        selected season has no succeeded run while the body names none. The
        detail of the second case is a fixed sentence.

Return one stored run with the table it projected.

``table`` is in projected table order, the order the worker prints, and it is
empty unless the run succeeded: a queued or failed run wrote no team rows, and
reporting a partial table would let a client read an unfinished simulation as
a finished one.

A path segment that is not a UUID is refused by the request validation, so
``/simulations/latest`` and ``/simulations/history`` are declared before this
route and are never read as identifiers.

The request issues two statements, the run with its season and, when the run
succeeded, the table. The season join is explicit because the models declare
no relationship the payload could lazy-load.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no stored run has ``run_id``. The detail is a
        fixed sentence and never repeats the identifier.

Return the table of one season, optionally cut off at a date.

Without ``season`` the answer is the season that starts latest among the
seasons with at least one match, which is the season a dashboard opens on
once ingestion has loaded it. ``as_of`` restricts the counted results to
the matches whose kickoff date is on or before it, the boundary included, so
a client can reconstruct the table as it stood after a given matchday from
the same endpoint that serves the current one.

The team set is every team that appears as the home or the away side in any
match of the season, whatever the status of that match, so a club whose only
fixture is still scheduled keeps a row of zeros and the table has the same
shape before and after the first matchday. The counted results are the
``played`` matches only: a scheduled fixture contributes nothing even when
its kickoff date has passed, which is the state of a postponed match the
source has not played yet. A season without a single match returns an empty
table with status 200, not an error.

The ranking is not computed here: the rows, their order, their points, their
tie-breaks and the form string all come from
:func:`lmi_core.standings.compute_standings`, called once with the team set
and the counted results. This module only decides which season, which teams
and which results the ranking sees, and maps the core rows to the payload.
``matches_counted`` is the size of the result list handed to it.

The request issues at most three statements: one to resolve the season, one
for the team set and one for the results, whatever the number of rows. The
team set is read with an explicit join on a union of the two team columns
because the models declare no relationship the code could lazy-load per row.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when ``season`` is given and no season has that code,
        or when no season has a match while ``season`` is absent. The detail
        is a fixed sentence in both cases and never repeats the client
        value, and the season and team endpoints follow the same rule.

Return every team, or the teams of one season.

Without ``season`` every stored team is returned. With ``season`` the answer
is restricted to the teams that appear as the home or the away side in at
least one match of that season, whatever the match status: a season whose
fixtures are not loaded yet is an empty list with status 200, not an error.
Only an unknown season code is a 404.

The ordering is by name, with the identifier as tie-break, so two teams with
the same name still come back in a stable order.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when ``season`` is given and no season has that code.

Return one team by its identifier.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no stored team has ``team_id``.

Return the focus view of one team in one season.

Three things are stored and served as they are: the team, the played
matches the form and the splits are counted from, and, when a simulation
succeeded, that run's row for the team. Everything else is derived on read.
The table row comes from :func:`lmi_core.standings.compute_standings` over
the season's team set and its played results, ``form`` and ``splits`` count
goals and points over the same matches, and the ``evaluation`` of every
upcoming prediction comes from :func:`lmi_core.live.scoring.evaluate`. No
ranking and no scoring rule is implemented in this module, so the focus view
cannot disagree with the standings, the predictions or the live metrics
endpoints.

``season`` selects the season; without it the season that starts latest
among the seasons with a match is served, exactly as the standings endpoint
selects it. The team has to appear in at least one match of that season,
whatever the status of that match: the focus view of a club that does not
play the season would describe a table row that cannot exist.

``standing`` is the team's row of the season table. The field is nullable
because the payload is also the shape a read over a partial table would
return, but the team-set rule makes it non-null for every team this endpoint
serves, so a null here means the read is broken rather than the data.

``form`` covers the last five played matches of the season, newest first,
and ``splits`` covers every played match of the season by venue, so the two
differ in scope and not in arithmetic. ``points_per_game`` is null for a
side that played nothing, because an average over no game does not exist.

``upcoming`` lists the team's next five fixtures still to be played, in
kickoff order, each with the standing forecast of every model stored for it.
The forecasts of all five are read in one statement and evaluated once, so
the number of queries does not grow with the number of fixtures, and a
fixture without a stored forecast still appears with an empty list.

``outlook`` is the team's row of the latest succeeded simulation run of the
season and is null when the season has no succeeded run, or when that run
stored no row for the team.

The focus items this resource deliberately does not carry: expected
points against actual points, rolling trends, top/middle/bottom splits, the
multi-season trend, the relegation race with its survival threshold, and how
much a result moves the relegation probability. Each of them needs a stored
input or a core rule this resource does not own, not another field here.

The request issues at most fourteen statements whatever the size of the
payload: the team, the season, the season membership, two for the season
table, two for the form, two for the splits, three for the upcoming fixtures
and one for the outlook. A request without played or scheduled matches
issues fewer, never more.

The return annotation is the response model, so no ``response_model`` is
passed.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no team has ``team_id``, when ``season`` names
        no stored season, or when the team plays no match of the resolved
        season. All three details are fixed sentences and never repeat the
        value the client sent.

Return the multi-season history of one club.

``team`` is the stored club. An identifier no stored club has is a 404; a
stored club that has played no match at all is a 200 with an empty
``seasons`` and an empty ``largest_drop``, because a club without history is
not an error and a line of zeros would invent a season it never played.

A season is listed exactly when the club played at least one match in it,
meaning a match with status ``played`` and both goal columns set. A season in
which the club only had fixtures, or none at all, is not listed. The order of
the seasons, the per-field denominators, the null-is-never-zero rule and the
drop rules are :mod:`lmi_core.analytics.history`'s and are not restated here.

``position`` is the club's place in the season's table as
:func:`lmi_core.standings.compute_standings` ranks it. The ranking receives
the same two inputs the standings endpoint uses: every club that appears as
a side of any match of the season, whatever that match's status, and the
season's played results. Both are read from the one statement that loads the
seasons' matches, so a history row can never contradict the standings
endpoint and no season needs a table query of its own.

Each counted match is the club's side of one played fixture: the stored
score flipped by venue, the expected points of the one eligible pre-closing
``1x2`` price when the fixture has one, and the shots, shots on target and
cards of each side flipped by venue. ``cards_for`` is the club's own yellow
plus red and is null only when the row carries neither value, which is why a
row that records zero keeps zero. A fixture without a statistics row leaves
every statistics field null, and one missing column stays null without
zeroing its neighbours. A closing price is never read, whatever its
bookmaker, because it is only known at kickoff, and a bookmaker outside the
priority of :data:`lmi_core.live.data.ODDS_PRIORITY` is not eligible.

The season lines and ``largest_drop`` are the output of
:func:`lmi_core.analytics.history.summarise` mapped field for field. Nothing
is rounded, re-sorted or recomputed here.

The request issues at most six statements whatever the number of seasons and
matches: the club, the seasons of its played matches, every match of those
seasons in one statement, the names of those clubs for the ranking's final
tie-break, the statistics rows of the club's played matches and their
pre-closing prices. The club's own rows are picked out of the matches
statement in Python, so no per-season query is issued. A club that played no
match stops after the first two statements and answers the empty history, so
the count never grows with the payload.

The return annotation is the response model, so no ``response_model`` is
passed.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no stored team has ``team_id``.

Return the relegation race of one club in one season.

``team`` is the stored club and ``season`` the resolved season code, so a
client can pass the code back to the other endpoints. An omitted season is
the season that starts latest among the seasons with a match, an unknown code
is the 404 ``Season not found``, an identifier no stored club has is the 404
``Team not found``, and a stored club that is not a side of any match of the
resolved season is the 404 ``Team not found in season``. Every detail is a
fixed sentence and none repeats the value the client sent.

``survival_threshold`` reads **every** stored season, not the resolved one:
the line answers what the league usually demanded to survive, and a sample of
the one season in front of the client would be the current table wearing the
name of a history. Each season is ranked by
:func:`lmi_core.standings.compute_standings` over its whole team set and its
played results, and one :class:`lmi_core.analytics.relegation.SeasonTable`
per season is handed to
:func:`lmi_core.analytics.relegation.survival_threshold` with
``relegation_positions=Qualification().relegation_positions``. The
configured count is the only relegation count in the repository -- the
simulator and the API build every run from it -- so a copy of it here would
drift from the qualification the stored runs were requested with. The
completeness rule, the counted place and the median are that module's rules
and are not restated here; the result is served field for field.

A ``None`` from the core function -- no stored season is a completed 20-club
season of 2005-06 or later -- is the 404 ``no completed season``. The field
is not nullable by design. Falling back to the current table, or serving a
zero, would read to a client as a survival line somebody computed out of a
sample that does not exist.

``rivals`` is the latest succeeded simulation of the resolved season, one
row per club, ordered the way
:func:`lmi_api.views.load_latest_simulation_outlook` orders the run it
describes: ``finished_at`` descending with the rows still missing that stamp
last, then ``as_of_date`` descending and finally the identifier descending.
Only ``succeeded`` counts. A queued, running or failed run measures nothing,
so serving its partial row would report a simulation that never finished.

The run's team rows become :class:`lmi_core.analytics.relegation.RankedTeam`
values and :func:`lmi_core.analytics.relegation.nearest_rivals` cuts them to
the subject club plus the :data:`_RIVAL_COUNT` clubs nearest to it by
expected position. The group is served in expected-position order with each
club's stored current points, mean points, relegation probability and the two
points quantiles, so the whole group reads in table order. When the selected
run holds no row for the subject club, ``rivals`` is served empty rather than
raising: the run exists and the club is simply absent from it, and ``run_id``
still names the run the rest of the answer was read from.

With no succeeded run the answer is still a 200: ``run_id`` and
``as_of_date`` are null, ``rivals`` is empty and ``series`` holds the season
code and no point, while the threshold and the remaining fixtures are served
as usual. A race without a simulation is a state of the data, not an error.

``series`` is :func:`lmi_api.views.load_simulation_history_points` of the
resolved season restricted to the rival identifiers, wrapped in
:class:`~lmi_api.schemas.simulations.SimulationHistory`. Restricting the read
is what keeps the series comparable: it is the group's history, not the
league's, and one point per as-of date of the season comes from the latest
succeeded run of that date. An empty group serves the season code and no
point, because there is no club whose history it would be.

``remaining_fixtures`` is the club's ``scheduled`` matches of the resolved
season, ascending by kickoff date and then identifier, each with the stored
fixture summary, the venue the club plays it at, and the opponent's position
in the resolved season's table. That table is
:func:`lmi_core.standings.compute_standings` over the season's team set and
played results, read out of the same all-matches statement the threshold
uses, so the two cannot rank the season differently. ``None`` is kept for an
opponent the table does not rank.

``p_win``, ``p_draw`` and ``p_loss`` are the latest succeeded run's
probability of the fixture's three results from the club's side: at home the
stored ``p_home``, ``p_draw`` and ``p_away``, away the same triple read from
the other end, so ``p_win`` means the club wins wherever it plays. They are
null when that run stored no probability for the fixture, which is the case
for a run created before revision 0004 and for a fixture the run did not
simulate.

``next_match`` is the first of those fixtures dated on or after Madrid today
(a postponed fixture dated earlier stays listed but is not next) and what each
of its three results does to the club, read from the same run's stored outcome counts
through :func:`lmi_core.analytics.relegation.next_match_swing`. Each outcome
carries the simulated frequency of the result, so ``p_outcome`` may differ
slightly -- about half a percentage point at 10 000 runs -- from the model
probability of that same fixture in ``remaining_fixtures``: the swing is a
frequency of the run's samples, the fixture triple is the model's
probability. Its ``current`` is the club's own row of that same run, so a
client computes every delta of the block against one consistent baseline.
The block is null when the core rule answers unknown -- a run created before
revision 0004, a stored match that is no longer the club's next fixture, or a
result the run never sampled -- and it is null as well when the run holds no
row for the club, because ``current`` is that row and a swing without its
baseline would misstate every delta.

The request issues at most eleven statements whatever the number of seasons
and fixtures: the club, the season resolution, every stored season, every
match of every season, the names of those clubs, the latest succeeded run
with its team rows and their club names, the run's fixture probabilities, its
next-match counts, the history runs, the history team rows and the fixture
summaries. The club's own fixtures and the resolved season's table are picked
out of the all-matches statement in Python, so no read here is one statement
per season or per fixture. Six of the eleven are conditional: the names read
is skipped when no match is stored at all, the fixture probabilities and the
next-match counts are issued only when the season has a succeeded run and the
club a remaining fixture, the two history statements only when the race has
rivals, and the summary statement only when the club has a remaining fixture.
A race over a season with a match, without a succeeded run and without a
remaining fixture stops after six.

The return annotation is the response model, so no ``response_model`` is
passed.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no stored team has ``team_id``, when ``season``
        names no stored season, when no season has a match while ``season``
        is absent, when the team is not a side of any match of the resolved
        season, or when no stored season is a completed one.

Return the season statistics of one team in one season.

``team`` is the stored club and ``season`` the resolved season code, so a
client can pass the code back to every other endpoint. The team has to be
part of the season's team set, which is every club that appears as the home
or the away side in any match of the season; a club of another season names
nothing this season can describe.

``played`` and ``points`` are the counters
:func:`lmi_core.analytics.season_stats.summarise` counts over the club's
played matches, which are the club's table row by construction: the table
counts the same played results of the same season, so a team can never read
one total here and another there. The ranking is not recounted here either;
it is read from :func:`lmi_core.standings.compute_standings` for the
season's team set and for the position each club holds in it. ``per_match``
is the team's own and its opponents' per-match average over exactly those
played matches, and ``league_avg`` is the same average over both sides of
every played match of the season, which is the comparison baseline the
payload promises.

``xpts_market`` sums the expected points of the matches that carry one, and
``xpts_coverage`` counts them. The expected points of a match are
:func:`lmi_core.analytics.season_stats.market_expected_points` of the one
eligible price row, seen from the club's venue: ``3 * p_home + p_draw`` at
home and ``3 * p_away + p_draw`` away, over the probabilities
:func:`lmi_core.modeling.market.remove_margin` derives, the only margin
removal in the repository. A fixture without an eligible pre-closing price
has null expected points and is left out of the sum and of the counter,
rather than contributing a zero.

The price is always *pre-closing*. The eligible rows are the ``1x2`` prices
with ``is_closing`` false from a bookmaker of
:data:`lmi_core.live.data.ODDS_PRIORITY`, and the selected row per match is
the most trusted of them, by the priority rank the live loader and the match
preview also apply. A closing price is never read, whatever its bookmaker:
it is only known at kickoff. One statement of
:func:`lmi_api.views.load_pre_closing_prices` reads every eligible row of the
club's played matches, ordered by fixture and then by that rank, and the
first row of each fixture is kept in Python. The priority list holds three
bookmakers, so a fixture can add at most three candidate rows: the read is
one statement and never one per fixture. PostgreSQL ``DISTINCT ON`` could
cap the rows per fixture in SQL, as the live loader does, but this read
keeps the candidates and picks the first of each fixture after the order has
ranked them.

``stat_coverage`` counts the matches that carry a statistics row and
``xg_coverage`` the matches that carry an expected-goals value on either
side. A played match without a statistics row is normal and stays absent:
it contributes its goals to the goals average and nothing to the other
fields, so a missing row never becomes a row of zeros. The same rule holds
inside a row: one missing column is null and is left out of that field's
mean only.

``splits`` is the season by venue, ``home`` counting the matches the team
played as the home side and ``away`` the ones it played as the visitor. Both
records come from the same ``match_record`` rule as the tiers, so the two
views cannot disagree on what a win is worth.

``tiers`` groups the team's matches by the opponent's position in the season
table, with the boundary and the membership of
:func:`lmi_core.analytics.season_stats.tier_members` and the counters of
``tier_records``: with ``n`` teams the top tier is positions
``1..ceil(n/3)``, the middle the next ``ceil(n/3)`` and the bottom the rest.
Each record carries the counters of every match against a club of that tier,
whatever the venue, and the tier's ``team_ids`` ascending. ``team_ids`` is
the membership of the tier, not only the opponents this team has already
met; a tier no club occupies is served as a record of zeros.

``matches`` is the chronological season, ordered by kickoff date and then
match identifier exactly as ``summarise`` orders it. Each row nests the
fixture summary and adds the venue, the points, the expected points, the
venue-scoped goals, the shots of both sides and the rolling form over the at
most five matches the club played on a date strictly earlier than its own.
That window never includes the match it describes and never another fixture
of the same day, because a stored date cannot order two fixtures of one day:
the form of a match is the form before its date, the same strict reading the
match preview applies. A row with no earlier match therefore has an all-null
rolling form, and so does a second fixture of the club's first day: a window
over no match has no average.

Every optional field means "not known", never zero. An average over an
empty set is null, a statistic no counted match carries is null, and a
group that played no match has a null ``points_per_game``. The coverage
counters are what lets a client tell an average of one match from an average
of six.

The request issues at most eight statements whatever the size of the season:
the team, the season resolution, the two of
:func:`lmi_api.views.load_season_standings` (the team set and the counted
results), the season's played matches, their statistics rows, the
pre-closing prices and the match summaries of the rows the payload lists. A
club that played no match of the season skips the price read and the
match-summary read, because both are bounded by the club's own played
matches. The statistics read is bounded by the season rather than the club,
because ``league_avg`` averages over both sides of every played match of the
season, so it is issued whenever the season has a played match at all.

The return annotation is the response model, so no ``response_model`` is
passed.

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 when no stored team has ``team_id``, when ``season``
        names no stored season, when no season has a match while ``season``
        is absent, or when the team is not a side of any match of the
        resolved season. All four details are fixed sentences and never
        repeat the value the client sent.
